claims.source: In addition to the V-ATPase subunits detected in the screen, we identified that TMEM199 was significantly enriched for gene-trapping insertions (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by genetic screen data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: TMEM199 is a putative transmembrane protein with 24% sequence identity to the yeast V-ATPase assembly protein Vma12p.
claims.source: TMEM199 is a putative transmembrane protein with homology (24% sequence identity) to the yeast V-ATPase assembly protein Vma12p (also known as Vph2p) (Hirata et al., 1993) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis and citation to Hirata et al., 1993.

claims.claim: Depletion of TMEM199 results in accumulation of the HIF1α reporter.
claims.source: Depletion of TMEM199 resulted in accumulation of the HIF1α reporter (Figure 2C), similarly to levels observed for depletion of the V-ATPase subunits (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Endogenous HIF1α only accumulates in the GFPHIGH population of TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells.
claims.source: FACS of the GFPLOW and GFPHIGH TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells followed by immunoblot showed that endogenous HIF1α only accumulated in the GFPHIGH population (Figure 2C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS and immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: Overexpression of CRISPR-resistant TMEM199 reverses HIF1α accumulation in TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells.
claims.source: Moreover, when we overexpressed a CRISPR resistant TMEM199 in these TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells, the accumulation of HIF1α was reversed (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E demonstrating rescue of the phenotype.

claims.claim: Most TMEM199 knockout clones are lethal after three weeks.
claims.source: We also isolated TMEM199 knockout (KO) clones, and while most TMEM199 knockouts were lethal after three weeks, a small number of clones that showed undetectable levels of endogenous TMEM199 by immunoblot had elevated HIF1α levels despite several passages (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations during clonal isolation.

claims.claim: TMEM199 knockout clones with undetectable TMEM199 levels have elevated HIF1α levels.
claims.source: We also isolated TMEM199 knockout (KO) clones, and while most TMEM199 knockouts were lethal after three weeks, a small number of clones that showed undetectable levels of endogenous TMEM199 by immunoblot had elevated HIF1α levels despite several passages (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Reconstituting TMEM199 knockout clones with overexpressed TMEM199 decreases HIF1α levels.
claims.source: Reconstituting these clonal cells with overexpressed TMEM199 decreased HIF1α levels (Figure 2F), further confirming the effect of TMEM199 depletion on HIF1α accumulation.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating rescue.

claims.claim: Human TMEM199 mutations have been associated with glycosylation defects.
claims.source: Human TMEM199 mutations have been recently associated with glycosylation defects (Jansen et al., 2016c), but the role of TMEM199 in V-ATPase function was not known.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2016c.

claims.claim: TMEM199 associates with V-ATPase subunits ATP6V0D1 and ATP6V0A2.
claims.source: Six proteins were identified as associating with TMEM199 with high confidence compared to the TMEM199 KO cells (Figure 2G). Of these, two were V-ATPase subunits, ATP6V0D1 and ATP6V0A2, which were also identified in the genetic screen (Figure 1A,C), and have been shown to associate with Vma12p in yeast (Graham et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2G and citation to Graham et al., 1998.

claims.claim: CCDC115 shows high structural homology to the yeast V-ATPase assembly factor Vma22p.
claims.source: A further protein, CCDC115 (coiled-coil domain-containing protein 115), was of particular interest as a 3-dimensional structural prediction analysis (Kelley et al., 2015) showed high structural homology to the yeast V-ATPase assembly factor Vma22p (Figure 2H) known to bind Vma12p (Graham et al., 1998), and human mutations in CCDC115 have been recently reported to show glycosylation defects (Jansen et al., 2016b) similarly to the TMEM199 mutations.
claims.evidence: Supported by structural prediction analysis shown in Figure 2H and citations.

claims.claim: Human mutations in CCDC115 show glycosylation defects.
claims.source: A further protein, CCDC115 (coiled-coil domain-containing protein 115), was of particular interest as a 3-dimensional structural prediction analysis (Kelley et al., 2015) showed high structural homology to the yeast V-ATPase assembly factor Vma22p (Figure 2H) known to bind Vma12p (Graham et al., 1998), and human mutations in CCDC115 have been recently reported to show glycosylation defects (Jansen et al., 2016b) similarly to the TMEM199 mutations.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2016b.

claims.claim: TMEM199 and FLAG-tagged CCDC115 interact as shown by immunoprecipitation.
claims.source: Immunoprecipitation of endogenous TMEM199 with FLAG-tagged CCDC115 confirmed the interaction identified by mass spectrometry (Figure 2I), and depleting CCDC115 from HeLa HIF1α-GFPODD cells stabilised the fluorescent reporter and endogenous HIF1α similarly to TMEM199 deletion (Figure 2J,K).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Depleting CCDC115 stabilizes the HIF1α-GFPODD reporter and endogenous HIF1α similarly to TMEM199 deletion.
claims.source: Immunoprecipitation of endogenous TMEM199 with FLAG-tagged CCDC115 confirmed the interaction identified by mass spectrometry (Figure 2I), and depleting CCDC115 from HeLa HIF1α-GFPODD cells stabilised the fluorescent reporter and endogenous HIF1α similarly to TMEM199 deletion (Figure 2J,K).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 2J and 2K.

claims.claim: Yeast Vma12p-Vma22p localize to the endoplasmic reticulum where they are involved in V-ATPase assembly.
claims.source: Yeast Vma12p-Vma22p localise to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where they are thought to be involved in V-ATPase assembly (Graham et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 1998.

claims.claim: TMEM199 is only present in the total membrane pool and not in the soluble fraction.
claims.source: Using cell fractionation experiments we observed that TMEM199 was only present in the total membrane pool and not in the soluble fraction (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell fractionation data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: TMEM199 localizes predominantly to the ER rather than endosomal or lysosomal compartments.
claims.source: Furthermore, immunofluorescence microscopy showed endogenous TMEM199 localised predominantly to the ER, rather than endosomal or lysosomal compartments (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: Endogenous TMEM199 co-localizes with HA-CCDC115 at the ER, although CCDC115 is mostly cytosolic.
claims.source: While it was not possible to visualise endogenous CCDC115 by immunoblot or fluorescence microscopy, we observed co-localisation of endogenous TMEM199 with HA-CCDC115 at the ER, although CCDC115 is mostly cytosolic (Figure 3D,E).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 form a complex at the ER, analogous to the yeast Vma12p-Vma22p V-ATPase assembly proteins.
claims.source: These results suggest that TMEM199 and CCDC115 form a complex at the ER, analogous to the yeast Vma12p-Vma22p V-ATPase assembly proteins (Graham et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Inferred from localization data, co-immunoprecipitation, and homology to yeast proteins.

claims.claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 deficient cells prevent EGFR degradation following EGF stimulation.
claims.source: EGF treatment stimulated the degradation of EGFR at 45 min in the control cells, with near complete loss of the receptor by 3 hr, consistent with prior reports (Mizuno et al., 2005) (Figure 4A–C). This degradation was prevented with BafA treatment (Figure 4A), confirming the role of the V-ATPase in the degradation of EGFR. However, EGF had no effect on the levels of EGFR in the TMEM199 or CCDC15 null cells, and no degradation was detected over 3 hr (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: Supported by EGFR degradation assay data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claims.claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 deficient cells prevent EGFR degradation similarly to BafA treatment.
claims.source: Indeed, TMEM199 and CCDC115 deficient cells prevented EGFR degradation similarly to BafA treatment (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of EGFR degradation data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Depletion of TMEM199, CCDC115, or core V-ATPase subunits partially rescues MHC Class I at the cell surface in K3-expressing cells.
claims.source: Therefore, we used HeLa cells expressing K3, which have low resting levels of cell surface MHC Class I (Figure 4D), and transduced these cells with sgRNA targeting TMEM199, CCDC115 or core V-ATPase subunits (ATP6V1A1, ATP6V0D1). Mixed populations of TMEM199 or CCDC115 deficient cells partially rescued MHC Class I at the cell surface (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: V-ATPase inhibition with BafA prevents acidification of endosomal compartments.
claims.source: However, live cell microscopy of HIF1α-mCherryODD reporter cells treated with BafA revealed Tfnr-phl within intracellular vesicles, confirming that V-ATPase inhibition prevented acidification of endosomal compartments (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by live cell microscopy data using pH-sensitive Tfnr-phl shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: TMEM199 or CCDC115 depletion prevents acidification of endosomes.
claims.source: Thus, TMEM199 and CCDC115 depletion prevents acidification of endosomes, similarly to BafA treatment or depletion of core V-ATPase subunits.
claims.evidence: Supported by Tfnr-phl fluorescence data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: V-ATPase inhibitors and the proteasome inhibitor MG132 result in similar levels of HIF1α accumulation.
claims.source: We therefore measured the levels of HIF1α in HeLa cells treated with different V-ATPase inhibitors in comparison to the proteasome inhibitor, MG132 (Figure 6A). Surprisingly, we observed similar levels of HIF1α accumulation following treatment with either V-ATPase inhibitors or MG132.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: BafA treatment increases HIF1α levels after just 4 hours.
claims.source: Furthermore, BafA treatment increased HIF1α levels after just 4 hr (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-course immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: HIF1α is only observed in the nuclei of cells treated with BafA or depleted of TMEM199.
claims.source: Rather than observing HIF1α accumulation within endosomal-lysosomal compartments, as would be expected following disruption of the V-ATPase, HIF1α was only observed in the nuclei of cells treated with BafA (Figure 6C) or depleted of TMEM199 (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: Nuclear increase in HIF1α following V-ATPase disruption is sufficient to activate HIF responsive genes.
claims.source: This nuclear increase in HIF1α was sufficient to activate HIF responsive genes, demonstrated by an increase in cell surface and total Carbonic Anhydrase 9 (CA9) when cells were depleted of TMEM199, CCDC115 or core V-ATPase subunits (Figure 6E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claims.claim: V-ATPase inhibition or depletion stabilizes HIF2α and the HIF target gene Heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1).
claims.source: V-ATPase inhibition or depletion also stabilised HIF2α in HeLa cells and the HIF target gene Heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) (Bertout et al., 2009) (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G and citation to Bertout et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Depletion of HSC70, LAMP2A, or ATG16 has no effect on HIF1α stabilization in aerobic conditions.
claims.source: To determine if CMA or macroautophagy played a significant role in the regulation of HIF1α in aerobic conditions, we examined the effect of depletion of HSC70, LAMP2A and ATG16 on HIF1α levels. Depletion of the CMA mediators, HSC70 and LAMP2A, or loss of the macroautophagy protein, ATG16, had no effect on HIF1α stabilisation in aerobic conditions (Figure 7A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claims.claim: BafA treatment still stabilizes HIF1α even when LAMP2A, HSC70, or ATG16 are depleted.
claims.source: Moreover, BafA treatment still stabilised HIF1α even when LAMP2A, HSC70 or ATG16 were depleted (Figure 7A,C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 7A, 7C, and 7D.

claims.claim: Only MG132 results in the accumulation of prolyl-hydroxylated HIF1α, while BafA and chloroquine stabilize HIF1α in a non-hydroxylated form.
claims.source: We measured the levels of total and prolyl-hydroxylated HIF1α in HeLa cells treated with several V-ATPase inhibitors, the proteasome inhibitor MG132, or the PHD inhibitor DMOG (dimethyloxaloylglycine) using a HIF1α prolyl hydroxyl-specific antibody (Figure 7E,F). While all inhibitors increased total HIF1α levels, only MG132 resulted in the accumulation of prolyl-hydroxylated HIF1α (Figure 7E,F). Conversely, BafA and chloroquine stabilised HIF1α in a non-hydroxylated form, similarly to DMOG treatment (Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claims.claim: BafA treatment markedly reduces PHD-mediated hydroxylation of HIF1αODD in vitro.
claims.source: Lysates from wildtype HeLa cells or cells treated with BafA for 24 hr were incubated with a purified His-tagged HIF1αODD protein for 15 min, and hydroxylation measured using the hydroxyprolyl-specific antibody. While HIF1αODD was rapidly hydroxylated in the wildtype HeLa lysate, BafA treatment markedly reduced hydroxylation (Figure 7G,H).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assay data shown in Figures 7G and 7H.

claims.claim: V-ATPase inhibition stabilizes HIF1α by decreasing PHD enzymatic activity rather than preventing lysosomal degradation.
claims.source: Thus, rather than preventing the lysosomal degradation of HIF1α, the V-ATPase inhibition stabilised HIF1α by decreasing PHD enzymatic activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the in vitro hydroxylation assay results and prolyl-hydroxylation status of HIF1α.

claims.claim: PHDs require Fe(II) and 2-oxoglutarate as cofactors for catalytic activity in addition to molecular oxygen.
claims.source: PHDs are 2-oxoglutarate (2-OG) dependent dioxygenases, which aside from molecular oxygen, require Fe(II) and 2-OG as cofactors for catalytic activity.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of PHD enzyme biochemistry.

claims.claim: Iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity.
claims.source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Semenza, 1993.

claims.claim: The V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin.
claims.source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kozik et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The V-ATPase is involved in the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes.
claims.source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983 and Straud et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The V-ATPase is involved in the release of iron from ferritin stores.
claims.source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mancias et al., 2014.

claims.claim: IRP2 is a sensitive marker of intracellular free iron that accumulates in iron deficient conditions.
claims.source: To examine if V-ATPase inhibition resulted in cytosolic iron depletion, we treated the cells with BafA and measured the levels of IRP2 (also known as IREB2); a sensitive maker of intracellular free iron that is rapidly ubiquitinated and undergoes proteasomal degradation in iron-replete cells, but accumulates in iron deficient conditions (Iwai et al., 1995; Salahudeen et al., 2009; Vashisht et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Iwai et al., 1995; Salahudeen et al., 2009; Vashisht et al., 2009.

claims.claim: BafA treatment stabilizes IRP2 similarly to cells treated with the iron chelator DFO.
claims.source: BafA treatment stabilised IRP2 similarly to cells treated with DFO (Figure 8A), consistent with V-ATPase inhibition leading to depletion of intracellular iron.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: BafA treatment increases NCOA4, the main cargo receptor for ferritinophagy.
claims.source: DFO and particularly BafA treatment also increased NCOA4, the main cargo receptor for the autophagic degradation of ferritin (ferritinophagy) and mobilisation of intracellular iron stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8A and citation to Mancias et al., 2014.

claims.claim: While NCOA4 promotes ferritinophagy in DFO treated cells, ferritin levels are unchanged in BafA treated cells, consistent with a complete block in autophagy when the V-ATPase is inhibited.
claims.source: However, while NCOA4 promoted ferritinophagy in DFO treated cells, ferritin levels were unchanged in BafA treated cells, consistent with a complete block in autophagy when the V-ATPase was inhibited (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing ferritin levels in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: TMEM199, CCDC115, ATP6V0D1, or ATP6V1A1 deficient cells show increased IRP2 and NCOA4 levels.
claims.source: Similar increases in IRP2 and NCOA4 were observed in FACS GFPHIGH populations of TMEM199, CCDC115, ATP6V0D1 or ATP6V1A1 deficient HIF1α-GFPODD reporter cells (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Disrupting V-ATPase integrity and assembly results in intracellular iron depletion.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that disrupting V-ATPase integrity and assembly results in intracellular iron depletion.
claims.evidence: Inferred from IRP2 and NCOA4 accumulation data.

claims.claim: Ferrous iron supplementation restores in vitro prolyl hydroxylation in DFO treated lysates.
claims.source: We first validated that ferrous iron restored in vitro prolyl hydroxylation of the HIF1αODD in DFO treated lysates (Figure 8C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assay data shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claims.claim: Addition of 1 µM Fe(II) completely restores prolyl hydroxylation of HIF1αODD in BafA treated lysates.
claims.source: We then examined the effect of ferrous iron treatment on PHD activity in extracts from BafA treated HeLa cells (Figure 8E,F). The addition of 1 µM Fe(II) completely restored prolyl hydroxylation of the HIF1αODD (Figure 8E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assay data shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claims.claim: Iron supplementation with 50 µM Fe(III) citrate completely prevents HIF1α stabilization in BafA treated cells.
claims.source: To explore if iron supplementation was sufficient to restore HIF1α turnover in cells where the V-ATPase had been inhibited, BafA treated HIF1α-GFPODD reporter or wildtype HeLa cells were supplemented with or without 50 µM iron (Fe(III)) citrate for 24 hr, and HIF1α levels measured by flow cytometry and immuoblot (Figure 9A,B). While BafA treatment stabilised the GFP reporter and endogenous HIF1α, this was completely prevented by the addition of iron to the media.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 9A and 9B.

claims.claim: Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover in DFO treated cells, although the concentration of iron needed is higher (200 µM Fe(III)) than for BafA treatment.
claims.source: Similar findings were observed in cells treated with DFO and iron citrate (Figure 9C,D), although the concentration of iron needed to restore HIF1α degradation was higher (200 µM Fe(III)).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 9C and 9D.

claims.claim: Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover in BafA treated primary human dermal fibroblasts, HEK293ET cells, and RCC10 cells reconstituted with VHL.
claims.source: Iron supplementation also restored HIF1α turnover in BafA treated primary human dermal fibroblasts, HEK293ET cells and RCC10 cells that had been reconstituted with VHL (Figure 9E–G).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 9E-G.

claims.claim: Iron citrate prevents the downstream activation of HIF1 target genes (GLUT1, VEGF, and carbonic anhydrase 9) following BafA treatment without affecting HIF1α mRNA levels.
claims.source: Furthermore, iron citrate also prevented the downstream activation of several HIF1 target genes (GLUT1, VEGF and carbonic anhydrase 9) following BafA treatment without affecting HIF1α mRNA levels (Figure 9J).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9J.

claims.claim: Iron citrate does not affect HIF1α stabilization following proteasome inhibition or in VHL null RCC10 cells.
claims.source: Consistent with iron supplementation only affecting HIF1α levels following V-ATPase inhibition, iron citrate did not affect HIF1α stabilisation following proteasome inhibition or in VHL null RCC10 cells (Figure 9G,H).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 9G and 9H.

claims.claim: Iron supplementation reverses HIF1α stabilization in mixed KO populations of V-ATPase subunits (TMEM199, CCDC115, or ATP6V1A1).
claims.source: Therefore, iron citrate was supplemented to the media of mixed KO populations of individual V-ATPase subunits (TMEM199, CCDC115 or ATP6V1A1) and HIF1α levels measured by immunoblot (Figure 9K–M). Iron treatment reversed the HIF1α stabilisation in the sgRNA-targeted cells (Figure 9K–M), confirming that iron supplementation was sufficient to restore HIF1α degradation following genetic disruption of the V-ATPase.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 9K-M.

claims.claim: Pre-conditioning the media with iron citrate does not prevent the accumulation of HIF1α following BafA treatment.
claims.source: We examined if treating cells with ferric iron prior to BafA treatment prevented HIF1α accumulation and conversely, also measured if iron supplementation after BafA treatment affected HIF1α levels (Figure 10A). Pre-conditioning the media with iron citrate did not prevent the accumulation of HIF1α following BafA treatment (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 10A.

claims.claim: Iron supplementation at the time of BafA treatment or after 12 hours decreases HIF1α levels.
claims.source: However, iron supplementation at the time of BafA treatment or after 12 hr did decrease HIF1α levels (Figure 10A), suggesting that iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover following disruption of the V-ATPase by a transferrin independent mechanism.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 10A.

claims.claim: Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover following V-ATPase disruption by a transferrin independent mechanism.
claims.source: However, iron supplementation at the time of BafA treatment or after 12 hr did decrease HIF1α levels (Figure 10A), suggesting that iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover following disruption of the V-ATPase by a transferrin independent mechanism.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the timing of iron supplementation effects.

claims.claim: Mixed KO populations of NCOA4 cells have no effect on HIF1α levels.
claims.source: To further explore the relative contributions of iron uptake and ferritin turnover to intracellular iron homeostasis, we depleted cells of transferrin receptor, IRP2 or NCOA4 by sgRNA, and used HIF1α stability as a sensitive functional measure of iron levels. Mixed KO populations of NCOA4 cells had no effect on HIF1α levels (Figure 10B,C – Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 10B, 10C, and supplement.

claims.claim: NCOA4 depletion increases IRP2 levels after 12 days, suggesting that IRP2 may increase iron flux through the endosomal pathway.
claims.source: Interestingly, NCOA4 depletion did increase IRP2 levels after 12 days, suggesting that IRP2 may increase iron flux through the endosomal pathway, but cell surface transferrin receptor and total ferritin levels did not change (Figure 10B,C)
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 10B and 10C, with interpretation suggesting increased iron flux.

claims.claim: Depletion of either IRP2 or the transferrin receptor stabilizes the HIF1α-GFPODD reporter and endogenous HIF1α, most markedly in transferrin receptor null cells.
claims.source: Depletion of either IPR2 or the transferrin receptor stabilised the HIF1α-GFPODD reporter and endogenous HIF1α, although this was most marked in the transferrin receptor null cells (Figure 10D–F,H – Figure 10—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 10D-F, 10H, and supplements.

claims.claim: IRP2 depletion does not alter cell surface transferrin receptor levels, consistent with IRP2 regulating iron flux rather than just transferrin receptor expression.
claims.source: IRP2 depletion also did not alter cell surface transferrin receptor levels (Figure 10D), consistent with IRP2 regulating iron flux rather than just transferrin receptor expression.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 10D with interpretation about IRP2 function.

claims.claim: Ferritinophagy does not contribute significantly to cytosolic Fe(II) levels when the transferrin pathway is functional.
claims.source: Thus, ferritinophagy does not seem to contribute significantly to cytosolic Fe(II) levels when the transferrin pathway is functional.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lack of HIF1α stabilization in NCOA4 depleted cells.

claims.claim: Iron treatment decreases HIF1α levels and increases ferritin stores in transferrin receptor deficient cells without altering NCOA4 levels.
claims.source: Mixed transferrin receptor KO populations were treated with iron citrate for 24 hr and HIF1α levels measured. Iron treatment decreased HIF1α levels and increased ferritin stores without altering NCOA4 levels (Figure 10G,H – Figure 10—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 10G, 10H, and supplement.

claims.claim: When the transferrin pathway is impaired, increasing the availability of extracellular Fe(III) is sufficient to restore PHD activity and HIF1α degradation.
claims.source: Thus, when the transferrin pathway is impaired, either by depletion of the transferrin receptor or disrupting V-ATPase activity, increasing the availability of extracellular Fe(III) is sufficient to restore PHD activity and HIF1α degradation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from iron supplementation rescue experiments in transferrin receptor deficient and V-ATPase inhibited cells.

claims.claim: Homozygous mutations in ATP6V0A3 cause infantile osteopetrosis.
claims.source: Homozygous mutations in a V0 subunit isoform (ATP6V0A3) cause infantile osteopetrosis (failure of bone resorption) (Kornak et al., 2000), while mutations in kidney specific isoforms (ATP6V0A4) cause distal tubular renal acidosis (Karet et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kornak et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Mutations in ATP6V0A4 cause distal tubular renal acidosis.
claims.source: Homozygous mutations in a V0 subunit isoform (ATP6V0A3) cause infantile osteopetrosis (failure of bone resorption) (Kornak et al., 2000), while mutations in kidney specific isoforms (ATP6V0A4) cause distal tubular renal acidosis (Karet et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Karet et al., 1999 and Smith et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Several cancer cell types express V-ATPase complexes at the plasma membrane, possibly as a mechanism for regulating cytosolic pH.
claims.source: Furthermore, several cancer cell types express V-ATPase complexes at the plasma membrane (Capecci and Forgac, 2013), possibly as a mechanism for regulating cytosolic pH, which appear to render tumour cells more susceptible to cell death when the V-ATPase is inhibited (Perut et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Capecci and Forgac, 2013 and Perut et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Cancer cells with plasma membrane V-ATPase appear more susceptible to cell death when the V-ATPase is inhibited.
claims.source: Furthermore, several cancer cell types express V-ATPase complexes at the plasma membrane (Capecci and Forgac, 2013), possibly as a mechanism for regulating cytosolic pH, which appear to render tumour cells more susceptible to cell death when the V-ATPase is inhibited (Perut et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Perut et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The ability of iron treatment to completely restore HIF1α turnover when the V-ATPase is inhibited argues against a role for CMA in HIF1α regulation.
claims.source: The ability of iron treatment to completely restore HIF1α turnover when the V-ATPase is inhibited, without altering the lysosomal degradation of EGFR or the autophagy cargo receptor NCOA4, also argues against a role for CMA in HIF1α regulation.

results.result: Genetic disruption of V-ATPase subunits stabilizes HIF1α in aerobic conditions. A forward genetic screen identified five V-ATPase subunits (ATP6AP1, ATP6V1A, ATP6V1G1, ATP6V0A2, ATP6V0D1) enriched for gene-trapping insertions. CRISPR-Cas9 depletion of these subunits and chemical inhibition with Bafilomycin A both increased HIF1α levels without affecting HIF1α mRNA expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C18, C22-C26 provide converging evidence from an unbiased genetic screen, CRISPR validation, and pharmacological inhibition. The genetic screen data (Figure 1A-C), CRISPR-Cas9 experiments (Figure 1D-E), and BafA treatment (Figure 1F-G) all demonstrate HIF1α stabilization. The lack of effect on mRNA levels (C27, Figure 9J) supports post-translational regulation.

results.result: TMEM199 and CCDC115 are mammalian V-ATPase assembly factors that stabilize HIF1α when disrupted. TMEM199 shows 24% sequence identity to yeast Vma12p, and CCDC115 shows structural homology to yeast Vma22p. Both proteins associate with V-ATPase subunits, and their depletion stabilizes HIF1α similarly to V-ATPase subunit depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C19, C20, C28-C32, C34-C35, C37-C38, C40-C41 are well-supported by genetic screen data (Figure 2A), sequence homology analysis (Figure 2B), CRISPR validation with rescue experiments (Figures 2C-F), mass spectrometry (Figure 2G), structural prediction (Figure 2H), and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 2I). The rescue experiments (C32, C35) provide strong evidence for specificity.

results.result: TMEM199 and CCDC115 localize to the endoplasmic reticulum and form a complex analogous to yeast Vma12p-Vma22p. TMEM199 is present only in membrane fractions and localizes predominantly to the ER. CCDC115 co-localizes with TMEM199 at the ER, though it is mostly cytosolic.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by cell fractionation (Figure 3A), immunofluorescence microscopy with quantitative colocalization analysis (Figures 3B-E), and comparison to yeast studies (C42). The ER localization is consistent with a role in V-ATPase assembly rather than function in mature complexes.

results.result: TMEM199 and CCDC115 are required for V-ATPase-dependent lysosomal degradation and endosomal acidification. Depletion of TMEM199 or CCDC115 prevents EGFR degradation and MHC Class I degradation similarly to BafA treatment. Live cell microscopy with pH-sensitive transferrin receptor demonstrates that depletion of these proteins prevents endosomal acidification.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by EGFR degradation assays (Figures 4A-C), MHC Class I rescue experiments (Figure 4D), and live cell microscopy with pH-sensitive Tfnr-phl (Figures 5A-D). The functional assays demonstrate that TMEM199/CCDC115 are required for V-ATPase function in both lysosomal degradation and endosomal acidification.

results.result: V-ATPase inhibition causes nuclear accumulation of HIF1α sufficient to activate HIF target genes. BafA treatment increases HIF1α levels within 4 hours to levels similar to proteasome inhibition. HIF1α accumulates in the nucleus rather than in endosomal-lysosomal compartments, and this is sufficient to activate HIF responsive genes including CA9, HIF2α, and HO-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by immunoblot comparisons (Figure 6A), time-course experiments (Figure 6B), immunofluorescence microscopy (Figures 6C-D), and flow cytometry/immunoblot analysis of HIF target genes (Figures 6E-G). The nuclear localization and functional activation of target genes demonstrate that V-ATPase inhibition leads to bona fide HIF pathway activation.

results.result: V-ATPase inhibition stabilizes HIF1α by preventing prolyl hydroxylation rather than through chaperone-mediated autophagy. Depletion of CMA mediators (HSC70, LAMP2A) or ATG16 has no effect on HIF1α stabilization. V-ATPase inhibitors stabilize non-hydroxylated HIF1α, while proteasome inhibition stabilizes hydroxylated HIF1α. In vitro hydroxylation assays demonstrate that BafA treatment markedly reduces PHD activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by CRISPR/siRNA depletion experiments (Figures 7A-D), prolyl-hydroxylation-specific immunoblots (Figures 7E-F), and in vitro hydroxylation assays (Figures 7G-H). The data clearly distinguish between proteasomal and lysosomal mechanisms and demonstrate that V-ATPase inhibition impairs PHD enzymatic activity rather than preventing lysosomal degradation.

results.result: V-ATPase disruption results in intracellular iron depletion. BafA treatment stabilizes IRP2 (a sensitive marker of iron deficiency) similarly to the iron chelator DFO. BafA treatment increases NCOA4 but ferritin levels remain unchanged, consistent with a complete block in autophagy. Genetic disruption of V-ATPase subunits (TMEM199, CCDC115, ATP6V0D1, ATP6V1A1) also increases IRP2 and NCOA4 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C68-C72 are supported by immunoblot analysis of iron homeostasis markers (Figures 8A-B). The accumulation of IRP2 provides strong evidence for iron depletion, and the pattern of NCOA4 and ferritin levels is consistent with impaired autophagy. The observation that genetic disruption of multiple V-ATPase components produces the same phenotype strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Iron supplementation directly restores PHD activity and HIF1α turnover following V-ATPase inhibition. Addition of 1 μM Fe(II) completely restores in vitro prolyl hydroxylation in BafA-treated lysates. Iron citrate (50-200 μM Fe(III)) prevents HIF1α stabilization and downstream target gene activation in BafA-treated cells across multiple cell types. Iron supplementation reverses HIF1α stabilization in genetic V-ATPase knockouts but has no effect on proteasome inhibition or VHL-null cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C73-C79, C81 are supported by in vitro hydroxylation assays (Figures 8C-F), flow cytometry and immunoblot analysis (Figures 9A-H), RT-qPCR (Figure 9J), and genetic rescue experiments (Figures 9K-M). The specificity of iron rescue (no effect on MG132 or VHL-null cells) and the dose-response relationship provide strong evidence that iron depletion is the mechanism linking V-ATPase inhibition to HIF1α stabilization.

results.result: Transferrin-mediated iron uptake is the predominant mechanism for maintaining cytosolic iron levels. Pre-conditioning with iron does not prevent HIF1α accumulation following BafA treatment, but concurrent or subsequent iron supplementation does, suggesting transferrin-independent uptake. NCOA4 depletion has no effect on HIF1α levels, while transferrin receptor or IRP2 depletion stabilizes HIF1α. Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover in transferrin receptor-deficient cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C91 are supported by time-course experiments (Figure 10A), CRISPR depletion studies (Figures 10B-F), and iron rescue experiments (Figures 10G-H). The differential effects of NCOA4 vs. transferrin receptor depletion provide strong evidence for the relative importance of iron uptake vs. ferritin turnover. The ability of extracellular iron to rescue transferrin receptor-deficient cells demonstrates transferrin-independent uptake mechanisms.

results.result: Background on HIF1α regulation and prior observations on lysosomal inhibitors. HIF1α is constitutively expressed but rapidly degraded by the proteasome following prolyl hydroxylation by PHDs and ubiquitination by VHL. Prior studies reported that lysosomal inhibitors can stabilize HIF1α, with proposed mechanisms including CMA, mitochondrial uncoupling, and V-ATPase-VHL binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C17 are primarily based on citations to established literature and provide context for the current study. These claims accurately represent prior knowledge and observations, though the current study challenges some of the proposed mechanisms (particularly CMA).

results.result: Background on V-ATPase function and PHD cofactor requirements. The V-ATPase is required for lysosomal degradation. PHDs require Fe(II) and 2-oxoglutarate as cofactors. The V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis through transferrin endocytosis, ferric-to-ferrous conversion, and ferritin degradation. IRP2 is a sensitive marker of intracellular iron.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C62-C67 are based on established knowledge and citations to prior literature. These claims provide essential background for understanding the experimental findings and are accurately represented.

results.result: Human mutations in V-ATPase components and assembly factors cause diverse diseases. Most TMEM199 knockout clones are lethal. Human mutations in TMEM199 and CCDC115 cause glycosylation defects and liver storage disease. Mutations in V-ATPase subunits cause osteopetrosis and renal acidosis. ATP6AP1 mutations cause immunodeficiency, and VMA21 mutations cause autophagic myopathy.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C36, C39, C92-C95, C111-C115 are supported by experimental observations (C33) and citations to clinical literature. These claims provide important context for the physiological relevance of the findings, though they are primarily descriptive rather than mechanistic.

results.result: Discussion and interpretation of findings. Iron rescue experiments argue against CMA involvement. The major consequence of V-ATPase inhibition is HIF1α stabilization by preventing prolyl hydroxylation. Findings are consistent with prior studies on V-ATPase and iron metabolism. Decreased transferrin uptake is the predominant mechanism. Transferrin-independent iron uptake can occur with sufficient extracellular iron. HIF activation and V-ATPase activity may serve as a feedback mechanism for iron control.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C110 represent interpretations and synthesis of the experimental findings. These are generally well-supported by the data presented, though some claims (particularly C107 about feedback mechanisms) are more speculative. The interpretations are logical and consistent with the experimental evidence.
